subject: penguin
pitch: An emperor penguin chick's proud parent. Glossy blue-black back and head, a crisp white belly blending into a warm golden-yellow patch at the neck and ear, a long slender beak with an orange-pink stripe, stubby flippers held slightly out, and big black feet. A fluffy grey chick peeks out from between its feet.
reasoning:
I'm planning the emperor penguin's skeleton structure, starting with the root hip joint and working out the spine chain, neck, head, flippers, and feet needed for a standing rest pose.

Then I work out an egg-shaped body built from a swept path along the spine chain, varying the radius at each point to get a rounder belly and narrower neck, with a slight forward tilt for a natural stance. I continue into the neck and head joint placement, and start thinking about how to shade the body with distinct colors for the dark back, white belly, and golden neck patch.

For the coloring, I'm defining a paint function based on surface normal and position: belly is white when the normal faces forward, back and sides go dark, and a gradient blends toward a golden-yellow patch on the neck and ear area, echoing the emperor penguin's coloring pattern.

I'll use a gradient paint transitioning white to gold for the front body, layering it so the head stays mostly black with ear patches as separate disc shapes, and keep the neck darker toward the back.

Setting the throat region black near the upper neck while keeping gold at the sides, with ear patches sticking out. Defining the color palette with blue-blacks for the body and darker tones for the head, then positioning the head joint and sphere scaled slightly flatter and longer to form the beak-forward shape.

Now I'm shaping the beak as a slender, slightly downcurved sweep from the head front to a narrow tip, tapering the radius toward the point and using a dark color with thin orange-pink stripe rods along the lower mandible, plus a separate pinkish-orange lower jaw sweep from its own joint.

For the eyes, I'm using small dark spheres with a tiny white glint sphere for highlight, maybe a dark brown eye ring, and I'm adding gold ellipsoid ear patches on the sides of the head using scaled spheres.

Adding a forehead taper sphere, then moving to flippers: I'll build them as stubby paddle shapes using a joint chain (shoulder, elbow, hand) and sweep a flattened elliptical cross-section along that path for a natural flipper silhouette.

For orientation, I want the flipper mostly flat and slanted down-outward, so I'm choosing outline axes that stay orthogonal to keep the extrusion well-defined rather than letting it skew.

Now I'm sketching the paddle shape as a sequence of points tracing out the flipper's tapered outline, with the width axis oriented outward-up along the slanted plane.

For rigging I'll build an arm chain with shoulder, elbow, and hand joints, extruding bone geometry at the shoulder and rotating the flipper slightly outward using a normalized direction vector. I'm also planning the coloring -- dark blue-black on the back with a white underside for the flippers, determining which faces get which paint based on normal direction.

Now I'm placing the shoulder joints near the body surface and planning the feet: flat black wedge shapes with three toes, positioned forward and hidden partly under belly feathers, built as an ankle-to-toes joint chain.

I'm placing the chick peeking out from under the belly, tucked between the parent's wide feet at the front, with its own small body and tiny feet resting on top of the parent's larger ones.

For coloring, I'm giving the chick the classic emperor penguin chick look: a black head with white facial patches and soft grey fluffy down covering its body.

For the fluff texture itself, I'll scatter small low-poly cones across the chick's body as cheap simulated down feathers instead of using complex card-based tufts. For the rig, I'm adding simple joints for the chick -- body, head, and a small connecting hierarchy nested under the parent's hip joint.

I'm skipping a separate jaw for the chick, just giving it a simple dark beak as a cone. I'm detailing the chick's appearance: a slightly elongated grey body sphere, a smaller dark head with white eye patches, black glinting eyes, and a small forward-pointing beak, tilted up as if peeking. I need to check that the chick doesn't overlap the parent's feet, so I'm adjusting the parent foot spacing and width so there's room between them for the chick.

I'm positioning the chick so it peeks out from beneath the parent's belly: raising the chick's body and head slightly and pushing the head forward in z so it clears the parent's torso silhouette, while letting the chick's body stay partly tucked and hidden. I'm skipping the idea of adding a brood pouch to keep things simple, and now I'm working out the radii along the parent's body path at different height levels.

Still shaping the body curve... I'm also sketching in a tail using a tapered wedge shape extending backward and down from the body, keeping it low and flat.

I'm checking the overall height stays reasonable for an emperor penguin proportion, then setting up the spine as a chain of joints rooted at hips, with the head attached at the end of that chain.

Thinking about splitting into separate spine and neck chains versus a single continuous path -- leaning toward one combined path for simplicity, with the head joint aimed forward at the top.

I'm considering extra surface detail like a darker sheen color for the back and possibly scattered feather scales, deciding whether to add a scale-pattern paint for texture.

Defining scale and gradient paints...

The white region extends about 65° from front, which feels right for a penguin's rounded belly coverage. I'll brighten the gold tone on the front side and verify the throat boundary sits correctly where the neck meets the head.

Now I'm working out the feet geometry: a wedge-shaped base box plus three toe boxes with claws, rigged to a foot joint bone.

Still writing foot and leg joint positions...

Shaping the webbed toe outline for the foot...

Working out the spacing between the parent's feet so the chick can stand between or on top of them without the toe overlaps looking wrong, factoring in the chick's body radius and foot positions.

Settling on leg x±0.115 with the foot joint positioned slightly forward and down, mostly hidden under the body silhouette at that height. I'm adding small ivory claw cones at the toe tips, oriented forward-down, against the dark foot color, then moving on to define the flipper joint chain starting at the shoulder position.

Now I'm computing the flipper's direction and extrusion length, working out normalized vectors so the elbow and hand joints land at the right offsets from the shoulder, checking perpendicularity between the length and width axes to make sure the chain geometry stays consistent.

I'm also planning the surface coloring: the underside facing forward should paint white while the side walls stay dark, mimicking a real flipper's pale belly and darker edges, with a rounded bevel where the flipper joins the body to avoid a harsh seam.

Now I'm positioning the jaw relative to the head and sketching the beak geometry—a slender, slightly downward-curving shape built from upper and lower sweeps tapering from base to tip, with the upper mandible colored dark and a pink-orange stripe running along the lower jaw sides.

Setting up the jaw joint with aim toward the lower beak, keeping the mouth closed in rest pose. Now I'm positioning the eyes symmetrically on each side of the head using a mirrored x-coordinate formula.

Adding small dark eye spheres with a tiny white glint for highlight, plus gold ear patches with a gradient shading from bright gold to pale yellow for the emperor penguin's cheek coloring.

Now I'm adding the baby chick figure, defining its joint hierarchy and body proportions as a grey rounded sphere attached to the parent hip joint.

For texture I'm scattering small cones over the chick body surface to simulate fluffy down, countershading the back and belly colors, then adding a darker head with a lighter facial mask for contrast.

I'm adding beady black eyes, a tiny black cone beak, and tilting the head joint slightly forward, then placing small dark feet boxes positioned so they don't overlap the parent's larger feet. I'm also checking that the chick head's position stays clear of the parent's belly curve by comparing their radii at that height.

Now I'm reworking the chick's placement so it's tucked under the parent's belly rather than sticking out in front, nudging the body and head z-coordinates back so the head is half-hidden behind the belly for a proper "peeking" look, while keeping the body visible below where the parent's belly radius narrows near the bottom.

Writing builder code...

Still refining radii...

Adding leg chains for both sides...

Adjusting toe lobe positions and outline coordinates...

Checking the flipper chain parented to the spine joint and shoulder position look fine, and I'm deciding to skip extra details like dorsal sheen or belly ruffle for simplicity. I'm also verifying imports are clean and settling on the paint callback signature before writing it out.

Setting beak colors with a darker upper and warm orange-pink stripes and lower section, scattering fluff cones on the chick body filtered by surface normal, and skipping extra head fluff to keep things simple before finalizing the output.
